name: Dirge-Permafrost
geological_features: Thick atmospheric ice fog reducing visibility to meters
Pressure ice formations where tectonic forces compress glaciers
specific_features: The Mourning Fog — a permanent ice fog so thick that the surface has never been fully mapped
Blind predators that navigate entirely by echolocation through the fog
resources: Dense atmospheric gases for industrial use
Pressure ice of unusual crystalline structure
description: Dirge-Permafrost is a cold, foggy ice world wrapped in a permanent atmospheric ice fog so thick that the surface is perpetually invisible from orbit. Visibility on the ground ranges from a few meters to a few hundred at best, creating an environment of claustrophobic, muffled isolation. The dense, cold atmosphere presses down with a weight that intensifies the oppressive feeling of being enclosed.

Sound behaves strangely in the fog — absorbed and redirected until its source becomes impossible to locate. Voices seem to come from everywhere and nowhere, and the grinding of pressure ice carries through the fog as a low, continuous moan that early explorers likened to a funeral dirge. The cold is severe but survivable with proper equipment; it is the psychological toll of the eternal fog that breaks most visitors.

Fauna has evolved to thrive in the blindness. Predators hunt by echolocation, sending clicks and calls through the fog and reading the returns with extraordinary precision. Their prey has counter-evolved acoustic camouflage, absorbing sound rather than reflecting it. The result is an evolutionary arms race fought entirely in the dimension of sound, producing creatures of remarkable acoustic sophistication but no visual complexity whatsoever.

The fog has prevented comprehensive surface mapping, and large regions of Dirge-Permafrost remain unexplored. Methane hydrate deposits beneath the ice are commercially valuable, but extraction operations in zero-visibility conditions are dangerous and expensive. The blind predators, while not typically aggressive toward humans, can be attracted by the acoustic signature of machinery, and several incidents have demonstrated that they are quite capable of disabling equipment they perceive as competing predators.
